clinician.final_diagnosis: lead perforation following pacemaker implantation, leading to iatrogenic intercostal artery perforation, a large haemothorax and life-threatening haemorrhagic shock
clinician.trajectory_summary: An early 80s woman presented to the ED two days after dual chamber pacemaker implantation with chest pain, rapid atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and decreased breath sounds on the left side. Initial labs showed Hb 130 g/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax identified a large left-side haemothorax and right ventricular lead perforation (E002). Upon transfer to a tertiary unit, her haemoglobin dropped to 103 g/L (E005). Pacemaker interrogation revealed low R wave amplitude and low impedance of the right ventricular lead (E006). A subsequent ECG-triggered CT scan revealed a massive accumulation of blood in the left pleura, mediastinal displacement, and active extravasation from the fourth left intercostal artery at the bone-cartilage junction. The tip of the right ventricular lead was located near the pericardium and directed towards the site of extravasation (E007). Multiplanar CT reformations further confirmed an extensive haemothorax, extravasation from the intercostal artery, and the perforating ventricular electrode pointing towards it (E008).

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with chest pain and decreased breath sounds on the left side two days after dual chamber pacemaker implantation.
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax identified a large left-side haemothorax and right ventricular lead perforation.
On arrival at the tertiary unit, the patient's haemoglobin level was 103 g/L, indicating significant blood loss from an initial 130 g/L.
Pacemaker interrogation revealed low R wave amplitude and low impedance of the right ventricular lead, consistent with lead dislodgement or perforation.

A subsequent ECG-triggered CT scan revealed a massive accumulation of blood in the left pleura, displacing the mediastinum to the right, with active extravasation from the fourth left intercostal artery at the bone-cartilage junction.
The tip of the right ventricular lead was located near the pericardium and directed towards the site of extravasation from the intercostal artery, linking the lead perforation to the arterial injury.
Multiplanar reformations of arterial phase CT imaging confirmed an extensive haemothorax and extravasation of contrast medium from the intercostal artery.

remaining_uncertainties: Explicit vital signs (e.g., blood pressure, heart rate) and clinical signs of hypoperfusion to directly confirm 'life-threatening haemorrhagic shock'.
Details of the clinical course and interventions (e.g., surgery, drainage, blood transfusion) following the critical CT findings.
